statement: Stickers cost 6 cents each. Tom pays using only 10-cent coins, and he must not get any change. What is the smallest number of stickers he can buy?

choices.misconception: I bought one sticker with one coin and forgot that he would get 4 cents back.
I found the number of coins he pays with, not the number of stickers.
I found that 10 stickers works, but there is a smaller number that works too.
I found how many cents he pays, not how many stickers he buys.

hints: Count up in sixes. When do you land on a ten?
With only 10-cent coins and no change, the total cost must be exactly 10, 20, 30 and so on. List the costs of 1, 2, 3 stickers and keep going until one fits.
The costs go 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first cost that is a whole number of tens is 30 cents.

solutions.reliable: List the cost: 1 sticker is 6 cents, 2 are 12, 3 are 18, 4 are 24 and 5 are 30. The first of these that is exactly some 10-cent coins is 30 cents, paid with 3 coins. So the smallest number of stickers is 5. The idea to keep: list in order and stop at the first one that works.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve: check the choices. 1 sticker costs 6 cents, which needs change. 5 stickers cost 30 cents, three coins exactly. 10 stickers also work, but 5 is smaller.

whyOnTest: It tests a careful list against a money rule, and two trap answers give the coins or the cents instead of the stickers.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
